exam: A 28‑year‑old woman with a new hard axillary mass and recent breast lump – what is the next investigative step and why? — Ultrasound of the axilla to characterise the node and guide core biopsy; it differentiates cystic from solid and assesses vascularity.

During a shoulder reduction you notice loss of radial pulse – what does this indicate and what immediate action is required? — Possible axillary artery injury or compression; call for urgent vascular assessment and maintain limb in neutral position.

A child presents with tender axillary nodes after a skin infection on the arm – how do you differentiate bacterial lymphadenitis from TB? — Look for acute onset, warmth, fluctuation and systemic toxicity for bacterial; TB shows chronic, painless enlargement, often with constitutional symptoms and may need GeneXpert if available.

Explain why Level III axillary nodes are less commonly sampled in breast cancer staging in low‑resource hospitals. — Access is deeper and requires more extensive dissection; limited pathology services often focus on Level I nodes which are sentinel nodes.

A patient with sickle cell disease develops a painful swollen axilla after a vaso‑occlusive crisis – what are the key differentials? — Bone infarction of the humerus, bacterial lymphadenitis, and splenic sequestration presenting with shoulder pain; clinical exam and CBC guide management.

Why is it important to assess sensation over the lateral forearm when examining the axilla? — It tests the C5‑C6 dermatome supplied by the lateral cord of the brachial plexus; loss suggests plexus injury.

In a malaria‑endemic area, a patient with severe anaemia has a bruised axilla after a fall – what life‑threatening condition must be ruled out? — Splenic rupture with referred bruising; assess for abdominal pain, hypotension and perform FAST ultrasound if possible.

What is the rationale for avoiding routine prophylactic antibiotics after a simple axillary lymph node excision? — The procedure is clean; antibiotics increase resistance and have no proven benefit in low‑risk patients.
ai.title: Axilla Anatomy and Clinical Significance
ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The axilla is the pyramidal space beneath the shoulder joint containing neurovascular structures, lymph nodes and fat. Understanding its anatomy guides safe procedures and diagnosis of regional disease.

b: Level I: lateral to pectoralis minor – contains cords of the brachial plexus.
Level II: posterior to pectoralis minor – houses the axillary artery and vein.
Level III: medial to pectoralis minor – contains the axillary lymph node chain.
sections.p: The axilla is a cone‑shaped space bounded anteriorly by the pectoralis major and minor, posteriorly by the subscapularis, latissimus dorsi and teres major, medially by the serratus anterior and thoracic wall, and laterally by the humerus. It is divided into three levels (I‑III) by the pectoralis minor.

b: Brachial plexus cords are named lateral, posterior and medial relative to the axillary artery.
The axillary artery becomes the brachial artery at the lower border of the teres major.
Sentinel lymph node biopsy for breast cancer targets Level I nodes.
sections.p: The brachial plexus, axillary artery, and axillary vein travel together, making the region vulnerable to trauma and iatrogenic injury. Lymph nodes here are the first drainage point for the breast, upper limb and thoracic wall.

b: Tender, enlarged nodes suggest bacterial lymphadenitis; common organisms include Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes.
Hard, fixed nodes raise suspicion for metastatic breast cancer or lymphoma.
Axillary artery injury presents with expanding hematoma, absent distal pulses, and cold limb.
sections.p: In low‑resource settings, axillary assessment helps detect infections, lymphadenitis, breast cancer spread, and complications of malaria‑related splenomegaly (splenic rupture may present with axillary bruising from trauma).

t.b: Is the node tender, mobile or fixed? Tender/mobile suggests infection; fixed suggests malignancy.
Absent radial pulse after trauma indicates possible axillary artery injury; urgent vascular assessment needed.
Detects fluid collections or vascular injury; if unavailable, rely on clinical signs and refer.

b: Inspect for erythema, ulceration or scar tissue from previous surgery.
Palpate from lateral to medial, noting size, consistency, mobility and tenderness of nodes.
Test sensation over the lateral forearm (C5‑C6) and medial forearm (C8‑T1) to assess brachial plexus injury.
Check radial pulse before and after shoulder abduction to detect arterial compression.
sections.p: When examining the axilla, use a systematic approach: inspect for skin changes, palpate for nodes, assess neurovascular status, and evaluate range of motion of the shoulder.

b: Confusing the axillary vein (compressible) with the artery (pulsatile).
Limiting node assessment to Level I only; TB or HIV can cause deep Level III enlargement.
Assuming all enlarged nodes are malignant without considering common infections (e.g., bacterial lymphadenitis, TB).
sections.p: Students often mistake the axillary vein for the artery, miss Level III nodes, or overlook systemic causes of lymphadenopathy.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly expanding axillary swelling with pain and loss of distal pulses
Hard, fixed axillary mass in a patient with breast changes
High fever, severe pain and overlying skin necrosis suggesting necrotizing infection
